GST/HST in the bank is not all business income: keep the tax reserve beside the cash ledger

Use four interactive charts to separate sales receipts, GST/HST received, eligible input-tax assumptions, a modeled remittance and cash remaining after the tax reserve.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Trace a hypothetical six-month GST/HST cash ledger

Interactive planning lab

Business cash funding position after month 6$31,700
Positive GST/HST amount still reserved at month 6$2,700
Cash position after that reserve, before other obligations$29,000

Original hypothetical six-month management ledger for an assumed GST/HST registrant using a simplified regular-method illustration. Sales, output tax, operating cash costs and input tax are separately entered monthly amounts. All invoices are paid and all expense/input-tax payments occur in the same month. The input-tax amount is assumed fully eligible, documented and claimed in the relevant period; eligibility is not tested. Months 1–3 form one model period and months 4–6 a second. At the start of month 4, the positive first-period net tax is remitted; a negative first-period amount becomes a separate potential receivable with no assumed refund cash during these six months. This is a chosen planning calendar, not a calculated statutory filing or payment deadline. Positive unsettled net tax stays within the bank position but is reserved; a receivable is not added to cash. No opening tax liability, owner draw, income-tax provision, payroll obligation, inventory, capital transaction, adjustment, quick method, tax rate or registration test is calculated. Negative cash positions are unfunded needs, not an assumed overdraft.

The central idea

Track sales-tax money separately from the customer payment total. A bank balance can include tax still owed, while a potential refund may not yet be cash.

01

Separate the sale from the tax within the same deposit

A customer payment can contain both the price of a sale and GST/HST charged on it. Both amounts may reach the same bank account, but the full deposit is not automatically business income available for an owner’s household spending.

CRA’s collection guidance states that collected GST/HST is held in trust until remitted. The first chart therefore splits the hypothetical monthly customer receipt into CAD 10,000 excluding tax and CAD 1,300 of separately entered GST/HST.

The example assumes a registrant and uses independently supported tax amounts as inputs. It does not choose a place-of-supply rate, decide whether a sale is taxable or test whether registration is required. These are management-ledger illustrations, not completed GST/HST returns.

02

Keep the input-tax assumption explicit

CRA’s net-tax guidance describes the regular method using tax collected or collectible and eligible input tax credits, with applicable adjustments. A business cannot assume every tax-looking payment qualifies for the same credit.

The default operating cash payment is CAD 6,000 excluding tax. Another CAD 400 is paid as GST/HST and assumed fully eligible, documented and claimed as an input tax credit in the relevant model period. The simplified monthly net-tax amount is CAD 1,300 − CAD 400 = CAD 900.

No adjustment or special method is modeled. If the entered tax paid would be only partly recoverable, or if the business uses a different calculation method, this simplified ledger does not establish the correct filing amount. Use the applicable records and method before treating the illustrated reserve as a real liability estimate.

03

Follow the bank movement before treating the balance as free cash

Each default month brings CAD 11,300 of customer cash and pays CAD 6,400 of operating costs including the separately entered input tax. The bank position increases by CAD 4,900. Of that increase, CAD 900 represents positive unsettled net tax in the illustration.

The other CAD 4,000 is the difference between receipts and operating cash payments excluding GST/HST. It is a narrow operating cash subtotal, not a calculation of taxable income or an owner’s after-tax pay. Income tax, payroll, capital purchases, debt payments and other commitments are outside this tool.

After three months, opening cash of CAD 5,000 has become CAD 19,700. The positive tax reserve is CAD 2,700, leaving a cash position of CAD 17,000 after that reserve. The two lines show these different readings of the same bank resources.

04

Paying an amount already reserved is not a second operating cost

The model groups months 1–3 into a first period and months 4–6 into a second. At the start of month 4, it pays the first period’s positive CAD 2,700 net-tax amount. This is an explicitly selected planning event, not a statutory deadline calculated from a reporting frequency.

The later bank position includes that payment once. By the end of month 6, the bank funding position is CAD 31,700. A new CAD 2,700 reserve has accumulated for the second period, so the position after that reserve is CAD 29,000.

The waterfall reconciles opening cash, receipts and payments. The closing reserve remains inside the bank amount; deducting it as a bank payment and then subtracting it again from closing cash would double-count the same obligation. The after-reserve metric performs the planning subtraction separately.

05

A potential refund needs a separate receipt assumption

Change the eligible input-tax assumption above the tax charged and received. The simplified net-tax result then becomes negative. The illustration tracks that amount as a potential receivable and reserves no negative amount from the bank.

At the first period boundary, a negative amount remains a separate potential receivable awaiting cash. The tool does not deposit it automatically in month 4. The second period’s negative amount also remains outside the bank total. This makes the cash needed to wait for a possible refund visible without promising an approval or payment date.

The eligibility assumption is still essential. A mathematical negative result does not establish that CRA owes the amount or when it will arrive. The cash ledger contains only the receipts actually assumed to have occurred, while the chart preserves the potential amount awaiting cash.

06

Connect the tax record to the business and household plan

CRA’s collection guidance notes that tax charged belongs in the reporting period covering the invoice date even if the customer has not yet paid. This model deliberately assumes invoices and related cash are received in the same month. It therefore does not solve the additional funding need created by unpaid invoices.

For an actual plan, keep the invoice record, collection date, eligible purchase-tax record and remittance calendar distinct. A tax reserve is also separate from the provision for personal or corporate income tax. The related self-employment guide addresses how business cash connects to an owner’s household draw.

The position after the GST/HST reserve is a useful intermediate number. Apply the other business obligations and household commitments before deciding what can leave the account. If the modeled position is negative, it identifies missing funding; it does not assume a bank will supply credit.
